title: The Matchmaker

jokes.text: Marylou to Tom Hanks: 'Oh, my God! You sound just like you do in the movies.' / Tom Hanks on hold: 'Stupid is as stupid does.'
jokes.setup: Marylou gushes that Hanks sounds just like he does in the movies — meaning he sounds like himself, a meaningless compliment
jokes.punchline: Tom Hanks responds in-character as Forrest Gump — 'Stupid is as stupid does' — implicitly agreeing with the inanity of what she said
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Marylou's fawning non-compliment is itself funny, and then Hanks weaponizes his own most famous movie line to gently (or not so gently) clap back. Economy is excellent — the punchline is four words and does double duty. The celebrity cameo elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Marylou
dialogue.line: Oh, my God! You sound just like you do in the movies. Stupid is as stupid does.

jokes.text: Marylou: 'Remember when you were in Bosom Buddies and you had that wig on?' — putting Tom Hanks on hold mid-sentence
jokes.setup: Marylou is supposed to be conducting a professional pre-interview with Tom Hanks but is instead fangirling about Bosom Buddies
jokes.punchline: She is so starstruck she puts him on hold mid-nostalgic question, making the incompetence complete
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe-comedy incompetence escalation. The Bosom Buddies reference grounds it in showbiz reality, and the abrupt hold is the perfect topper. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Marylou
dialogue.line: Remember when you were in bosom buddies and you had that wig on?

jokes.text: Paula to Marylou: 'I don't wanna hurt your feelings, OK? But clearly, you suck at this job. And if you don't get better, you're gonna get fired. This is not the cat counter at Petco, OK?'
jokes.setup: Paula steps in to rescue the Tom Hanks call professionally
jokes.punchline: She delivers a devastatingly blunt performance review to Marylou ending with the oddly specific 'cat counter at Petco' comparison
jokes.explanation: The 'cat counter at Petco' is a genuinely funny, specific insult — it's not just a random job, it's a job with a specific mundane absurdity (there's a counter for cats?). The setup of 'I don't wanna hurt your feelings' followed by immediate brutality is a great structure. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: This is not the cat counter at petco, OK?

jokes.text: Hank to Brian: 'Why didn't you call Shadow Stevens and tell him about the poker game last night?' / Brian says he left a message / Hank: 'That's the old number.' / Brian: 'I'm sorry.' / Hank: 'The new number's in your rolodex, Brian.' / Brian: 'I'm sorry.' / Hank: 'Are you crying?'
jokes.setup: Hank delivers a standard workplace dressing-down about a missed message
jokes.punchline: Brian, processing a breakup, starts crying at mild criticism — Hank's incredulous 'Are you crying?' punctuates the tonal mismatch
jokes.explanation: The slow build of Hank's mundane complaint crashing into Brian's emotional fragility is good Larry Sanders cringe. Hank's obliviousness is perfectly in character. 'Are you crying?' as the punchline is economical and perfectly delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Are you crying?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Please, don't do that.

jokes.text: Hank berates Brian for using the wrong phone number from the Rolodex; Brian begins crying at the mild criticism.
jokes.setup: Hank is doing a standard boss-employee dressing-down about a missed poker game invite
jokes.punchline: Brian starts crying, completely disproportionate to the offense — Hank is bewildered
jokes.explanation: Effective setup for the Brian/David storyline. The comedy is in the tonal gap — Hank's bureaucratic frustration about a Rolodex entry versus Brian's tearful breakdown. Gains rewatch value once the context is revealed. Not a standalone joke but plants the episode's emotional engine.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: His boyfriend, Hank. They've been together for over a year and a half.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, my God. I didn't know that.

jokes.text: Beverly to Hank: Brian broke up with 'David' / Hank: 'David?' / Beverly: 'His boyfriend, Hank.'
jokes.setup: Hank discovers he's been dressing down an emotionally devastated employee without knowing why
jokes.punchline: Hank didn't even know Brian was gay — Beverly has to explain 'His boyfriend, Hank' with the weary patience of someone who tells Hank obvious things constantly
jokes.explanation: Hank's self-absorption making him oblivious to his assistant's personal life for over a year is funny and character-consistent. Beverly's exasperated clarification 'His boyfriend, Hank' is the perfectly calibrated punchline — three words that contain all the weariness.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, that makes one of us.

jokes.text: Larry (after new PA compliments last night's show): 'Well, that makes one of us.'
jokes.setup: New PA Marylou says working on the show is 'a dream come true' and compliments Larry's performance
jokes.punchline: Larry's instantly deflating self-deprecation — 'Well, that makes one of us'
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Larrian — self-pitying, instantly deflating sincere warmth, and economical. 'That makes one of us' is six words that communicate Larry's entire character: his anxiety about his own show, his inability to accept compliments, and his dark humor. Character integration earns a high score.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: God! Kiss ass much?

jokes.text: Marylou says she hoped she asked all the questions Larry would ask. Hank: 'Did you ask if she'd sleep with you? 'Cause then you nailed it.'
jokes.setup: Marylou nervously says she hoped her pre-interview questions matched Larry's interests
jokes.punchline: Hank reveals that Larry's primary interest in female guests is whether they'll sleep with him
jokes.explanation: Great character joke about Larry's ego and libido. Hank delivering this completely matter-of-factly as insider knowledge is what makes it work — it's not a joke to Hank, it's just the truth. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Did you ask if she'd sleep with you? 'Cause then you nailed it.

jokes.text: Hank looks at Brian's face and says 'Mmm, missed a spot.' Brian: 'No, on your face.'
jokes.setup: Brian asks Hank 'How do I look?' before the audience warm-up, presumably as emotional reassurance
jokes.punchline: Hank takes the question literally and critiques his shave; Brian redirects him to what he actually meant
jokes.explanation: A functional misunderstanding gag. Hank takes an emotional question as purely physical — consistent with his character. Not a standout but earns a chuckle.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Mmm, missed a spot. No, on your face.

jokes.text: Larry on-air tells Nicolette Sheridan: 'I saw you in that TV movie Mother, May I Sleep with Danger? You were sensational, if I may say.'
jokes.setup: Larry is flattering a celebrity guest on-air with effusive praise about her work
jokes.punchline: Nicolette Sheridan replies: 'Um, Larry, I wasn't in that movie.' — a pause moment where the floor falls out
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first major set piece and it earns its high score. The setup is meticulous — Larry gushing on live TV with total confidence — and the punchline is delivered with maximum awkward silence before Nicolette's gentle correction. 'Mother, May I Sleep with Danger?' is itself an absurdly specific B-movie title that gets an extra laugh. The situation is deeply Larrian: his ego writing checks his staff's incompetence can't cash, live on air. Justifies the 8+ range.

dialogue.speaker: Nicolette Sheridan
dialogue.line: Um, Larry, I wasn't in that movie.

jokes.text: Larry's on-air recovery: 'Well, then, what movie... I know you're great, and I'm a gigantic fan, and I saw you in, uh, this movie, uh... that... which movie am I thinking of? Which one? Well, why don't we take a break, and we'll come right back, and we'll figure out which movie I'm thinking of.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just been corrected on-air and tries to recover
jokes.punchline: His recovery is to just... keep going deeper into the hole, suggesting they take a break to 'figure out which movie I'm thinking of' — turning live TV incompetence into a scheduled segment
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic peak in its first act. Larry's 'recovery' escalates the original humiliation by institutionalizing it — 'we'll come right back and we'll figure out which movie I'm thinking of' is an absurdist non-solution that only makes the situation worse. It's deeply character-specific: only Larry Sanders would respond to public humiliation with performative confidence that makes it worse. The structure is superb: each phrase digs deeper. This is exceptional sitcom writing that earns an 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, why don't we take a break, and we'll come right back, and we'll figure out which movie I'm thinking of.

jokes.text: Nicolette: 'I've been off for 3 years. You've gotta remember that.' Larry: 'We'll be right back, no flipping.'
jokes.setup: Larry has failed to cover his ignorance; Nicolette bluntly reminds him she hasn't worked in three years
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately cuts to commercial with the reflexive host phrase 'no flipping' — fleeing the scene
jokes.explanation: 'No flipping' is a perfect punctuation mark on the disaster. The autopilot host-voice kicking in exactly when Larry most wants to escape is a masterful comedic instinct. The specificity of 'no flipping' as a period-accurate network phrase adds a layer of media satire.

dialogue.speaker: Nicolette Sheridan
dialogue.line: I've been off for 3 years. You've gotta remember that.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I just told Nicolette Sheridan that she was great in a movie, it turned out I was talking about Tori Spelling.'
jokes.setup: Larry explains backstage what happened on-air
jokes.punchline: The reveal that he confused Nicolette Sheridan with Tori Spelling adds a second layer of insult — not just wrong movie, wrong actress entirely
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the original mistake — wrong movie AND wrong actress — is a good comedic reveal. Confusing a Baywatch actress with Tori Spelling is its own specific insult to Nicolette Sheridan. Good situational comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Did I do something wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Yes.

jokes.text: Larry, spiraling into self-doubt backstage: 'Was it my bad breath? Because, um, I ate an avocado today... but avocados don't give you bad breath.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just been told the notes were wrong and Nicolette probably won't date him now
jokes.punchline: Larry's instant pivot to whether his bad breath ruined his romantic chances — then self-reassurance that avocados don't cause bad breath
jokes.explanation: Wonderfully Larrian spiral of narcissism and neurosis. While everyone else is focused on the professional failure, Larry is worried about a date. The avocado specificity is the cherry on top — his self-reassurance about avocado breath mid-crisis is perfectly absurd and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, yes. Yes, I watch everything on this magic box.

jokes.text: Artie: 'If people only knew.' — reaction beat as Hank wanders off still obsessing about his seat
jokes.setup: Hank has been fussing about whether his breath/appearance is the reason for a romantic failure, completely missing the point
jokes.punchline: Artie's muttered 'If people only knew' — about the chaos behind the glamorous late-night TV facade
jokes.explanation: Classic Artie dry aside — the veteran producer as Greek chorus. Four words that contain the entire show's premise. Not a marquee joke but reliable texture.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I just told Nicolette Sheridan that she was great in a movie, it turned out I was talking about Tori Spelling.

jokes.text: Larry live on-air with Nicolette Sheridan: 'I think that we've talked enough about your career, which is going so wonderfully.' — then immediately pivots to 'I understand you were just in Rome.' / Nicolette: 'Paris.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to recover from the movie gaffe by pivoting to personal life questions, using his (still-wrong) notes
jokes.punchline: He gets the city wrong too — 'Rome' / 'Paris' — the third consecutive factual error from the same bad prep
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation of the wrong-notes running gag. The audience now knows the notes are bad, so when Larry says 'Rome,' there's anticipatory comedy before Nicolette even says 'Paris.' Economy is high — the entire joke is one word vs. one word. Classic Larry Sanders structural compression.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Was it my bad breath? Because, um, I ate an avocado today... but avocado's don't give you bad breath.

jokes.text: Paula to Marylou: 'Marylou is your friend. She's still learning, but this is the second time that Larry's been embarrassed because her notes have been wrong, and this has got to stop.' — then cut to Marylou getting the same speech verbatim from Paula
jokes.setup: Paula delivers a serious corrective speech to someone (presumably Hank) about Marylou
jokes.punchline: The next scene is Paula delivering the EXACT same speech word-for-word directly to Marylou — implying she's rehearsed this same confrontation or that the show is repeating itself with metatextual awareness
jokes.explanation: A structural joke about the repetition of workplace management — Paula giving the same speech twice, or having given it once off-screen and now giving it to the actual target. The verbatim repetition is the joke, and it works as a scene cut comedy beat. Rewards attentive viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: If people only knew.

jokes.text: Marylou's defense: 'Nicolette is wrong, too. Because that movie isn't even listed in Tori Spelling's bio. Do you know why? 'Cause this is Tori Amos' bio. Tori Amos is a singer, not an actor.'
jokes.setup: Marylou is being held responsible for the wrong pre-interview notes
jokes.punchline: Her defense reveals not just one but TWO errors layered on each other — she confused Tori Spelling with Tori Amos, a singer with no acting credits
jokes.explanation: Brilliant escalation. We thought the mistake was wrong movie → Tori Spelling. Now we learn the notes weren't even TORI SPELLING's — they were TORI AMOS, a musician. Each layer is funnier than the last. The specificity (Tori Amos is a singer, not an actor — delivered as if this is marginally helpful information) is great. This is the kind of nested comedy mistake that rewards The Larry Sanders Show's density. Justifies the high score.

dialogue.speaker: Nicolette
dialogue.line: Paris.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Paula... I know. I heard.

jokes.text: Brian asks 'Go where?' / Hank: 'Wherever the fucking horse goes.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just delivered his horse cliché with total confidence
jokes.punchline: Brian's innocent literal question 'Go where?' exposes the emptiness of the metaphor; Hank doubles down — 'Wherever the fucking horse goes' — adding profanity for gravitas
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's standout jokes. 'Wherever the fucking horse goes' is instantly quotable and works on multiple levels: it exposes the hollowness of clichéd advice while being perfect Hank — he responds to having his metaphor questioned not by admitting its emptiness but by doubling down with profanity-enhanced authority. The setup/punchline structure across two jokes is excellent. Economy: five words, maximum payload. Fully justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Marylou
dialogue.line: 'Cause this is Tori Amos' bio. Tori Amos is a singer, not an actor.

jokes.text: Hank at the bar: 'There's a guy looking at you. No. Don't. Don't. Don't look. No, he's, um, he's at the end of the bar. He's, uh, very attractive.'
jokes.setup: Hank has brought Brian to a bar for a confidence boost after a breakup
jokes.punchline: Hank is now actively playing matchmaker in a gay bar, whispering about an attractive man — a complete role reversal from the oblivious boss
jokes.explanation: Hank in wingman mode at a gay bar is inherently comic given his character. His enthusiasm and specific 'very attractive' assessment show him fully committed to the bit while completely unaware of how he reads to others.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You get back on the horse. You get back on the horse and you go.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: Go where?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Wherever the fucking horse goes.

jokes.text: Hank approaches Gordon: 'Oh, my go... do you know who you are?' / Gordon: 'Yes I do. Do you know who you are?' / Hank: 'Yes. I'm Gordon.'
jokes.setup: Hank approaches a man at the bar with his celebrity opener, expecting to be recognized
jokes.punchline: Gordon turns the question back on him; Hank confidently says 'Yes. I'm Gordon' — accidentally giving Gordon's own name, a Freudian self-erasure
jokes.explanation: The moment where Hank says 'Yes. I'm Gordon' when he clearly means 'Yes, I'm Hank Kingsley' is a beautiful verbal pratfall — either he's confused or he's so rattled his brain short-circuits. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Gordon
dialogue.line: Oh, my go... do you know who you are?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yes I do.

dialogue.speaker: Gordon
dialogue.line: Do you know who you are?

jokes.text: Gordon's friend Alan: 'You are very popular in the gay community, Hank.' / Hank (to Brian): 'See, I told ya.'
jokes.setup: Hank is being told he's popular in the gay community
jokes.punchline: Hank's immediate 'See, I told ya' — taking pride in gay community popularity as validation, without registering any irony given his subsequent panic
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is rich: Hank will panic about being seen in gay bars in the very next scene, but here he preens at the validation. 'See, I told ya' is the exact wrong response from someone who'll soon be desperate to seem straight. Character comedy at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Gordon
dialogue.line: You are very popular in the gay community, Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: See, I told ya.

jokes.text: Hank explains to Gordon: 'Well, Brian broke up with his boyfriend, and so I thought I'd take him out and show him a good time here... we were just sitting, and, uh, talking about getting back on the horse, when we saw you staring.'
jokes.setup: Hank is introducing himself and Brian to men in a gay bar
jokes.punchline: He casually, obliviously describes a scenario (taking a heartbroken gay man to a gay bar to get back on the horse) that makes him sound like he's on a gay date himself — and accuses the man of staring
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'getting back on the horse' in this context is funny — the metaphor now applies to gay dating, and Hank has no idea. His accusation that Gordon was 'staring' is a nice reversal.

dialogue.speaker: Gordon
dialogue.line: Staring? Really?

jokes.text: Gordon's reaction: 'Staring? Really?' — Gordon and Alan make polite excuses and leave quickly
jokes.setup: Hank has just been cheerfully oblivious and accused Gordon of staring
jokes.punchline: Gordon's polite 'Staring? Really?' followed by the swift exit — the social horror of the situation finally landing
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat — the social crash of Hank's obliviousness. Not a standout moment but necessary pacing.

dialogue.line: Sidekick by day, gay caballero by night.

jokes.text: Brian after Gordon and Alan leave: 'See? I'm a loser.' / Hank: 'You're not gonna cry again, are ya?'
jokes.setup: Brian is dejected after the failed encounter
jokes.punchline: Hank's callback to Brian's earlier crying — 'You're not gonna cry again, are ya?' — showing Hank's only real concern is not having to deal with more tears
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the earlier crying beat. Hank's emotional incompetence is consistent and the callback is economical. Not the funniest line but earns credit for character consistency.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, that's a lie. We never went to mother lode.

jokes.text: Army Archer's Variety column read aloud: 'Larry Sanders' sidekick Hank Kingsley was seen getting a few kicks of his own last night. Kingsley was painting the town red at several well-known gay bars, including, uh, Rage, Spike, and Mother Lode.'
jokes.setup: Hank was just innocently helping his heartbroken assistant
jokes.punchline: The Variety column has him listed as touring multiple named gay bars — specific real LA venues — with the showbiz gossip column's clinical neutrality making it funnier
jokes.explanation: The formal Variety column prose applied to gay bar tourism is genuinely funny — 'painting the town red at several well-known gay bars' is a perfect sentence. The specificity of naming real LA gay bars (Rage, Spike, Mother Lode) grounds it in the show's insider Hollywood realism.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yes! Yes! Rayneene, perfect.

jokes.text: Hank's immediate response to the Variety column: 'Well, that's a lie. We never went to Mother Lode.'
jokes.setup: Hank is hearing his gay bar tour reported in the press
jokes.punchline: His only objection is factual accuracy about which bars he visited — not the implication itself
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and fully earns the 8+ score. The comedy comes from Hank's complete prioritization of factual accuracy over the larger reputational catastrophe — he's not saying 'I'm not gay,' he's saying 'I didn't go to THAT bar.' This is sophisticated character comedy: Hank's narcissism makes him focus on being quoted incorrectly rather than the implication. Economy is near-perfect. Totally quotable and deeply character-specific.

dialogue.line: Rock hudson was gay.

jokes.text: The column's phrase: 'Sidekick by day, gay caballero by night.'
jokes.setup: Army Archer's column is describing Hank's evening
jokes.punchline: 'Gay caballero' — a wordplay on 'gay' (both senses) and the Spanish for 'gentleman/knight,' riffing on the old cowboy archetype
jokes.explanation: A witty piece of in-universe celebrity gossip writing. 'Gay caballero' is a clever double-meaning phrase that works as good wordplay and as mockery of Hollywood gossip column style.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Tell her to wear something very short and very tight.

jokes.text: Hank's plan: 'I have to find an attractive woman to be seen with.'
jokes.setup: Hank is reacting to the Variety column
jokes.punchline: His solution to being outed is the classic Hollywood beard strategy — delivered as if this is entirely reasonable
jokes.explanation: Setup for the Rock Hudson joke. Functional as a beat but the payoff is where the gold is.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Conway
dialogue.line: Well, I'd like my car detailed.

jokes.text: Hank: 'The studios used to make sure that Rock Hudson was seen in the company of beautiful women all the time. That way people would know that he was a romantic leading man.' / Beverly: 'Rock Hudson was gay.'
jokes.setup: Hank explains his Hollywood beard strategy by citing the Rock Hudson precedent as evidence that it WORKS
jokes.punchline: Beverly calmly informs him that Rock Hudson — his example of successful image management — was, famously, gay
jokes.explanation: The episode's comedic peak. Structurally perfect: Hank builds an elaborate, confident argument using Rock Hudson as proof of concept, then Beverly demolishes it in four words. 'Rock Hudson was gay' is one of the most efficiently devastating punchlines in the episode. The joke works because Hank's argument was ALMOST internally logical — you follow his reasoning, then the rug pull is total. Character integration is exceptional: only Hank Sanders would cite Rock Hudson as evidence that bearding works. Beverly's deadpan delivery is the perfect straight-man punctuation. Fully justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Conway
dialogue.line: I, uh, got the trainee, right?

jokes.text: Beverly's reaction to the Rock Hudson revelation moment: 'I'll get right on this.' — immediately moving on to execute Hank's now-undermined plan
jokes.setup: Beverly has just destroyed Hank's argument with four words
jokes.punchline: She immediately and professionally pivots to executing his plan anyway — 'I'll get right on this' — as if the Rock Hudson point never happened
jokes.explanation: The topper to the Rock Hudson joke. Beverly's professional pivot after delivering the most devastating fact-check of the scene is a perfect button. The joke is in the lack of reaction — she's moved on, Hank is presumably processing.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: What is wrong with you? Nicolette sheridan was on the show last night.

dialogue.speaker: Marylou
dialogue.line: I know, but she's on my calendar for tonight, too.

jokes.text: Tim Conway arriving: 'I'd like my car detailed.' — responding to Marylou being introduced as the person to call if he needs anything
jokes.setup: Larry introduces Marylou as available to help Tim Conway with anything he needs
jokes.punchline: Conway immediately asks for his car to be detailed — treating the network pre-interview assistant as a valet service
jokes.explanation: Good celebrity-specific comedy. Tim Conway immediately subverting Marylou's professional role with a mundane car request is funny — equal parts about Conway's showbiz entitlement and Marylou's awkward 'I'll look into that' response.

dialogue.speaker: Marylou
dialogue.line: Tied up. And, uh, harriet? Tied up.

jokes.text: Conway to Paula about Marylou: 'I got the trainee, right?' / Paula: 'She's great. Don't worry about it.' / Conway: 'I can imagine.'
jokes.setup: Tim Conway can tell from the car-detailing moment that Marylou is not a seasoned professional
jokes.punchline: 'I can imagine' — the driest possible acceptance of Paula's reassurance, conveying complete disbelief in two words
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan. 'I can imagine' is two words that contain a complete devastating assessment. Economy is the joke's strength.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Conway
dialogue.line: He'll ask me about speed 2! I'll fill in! I'll have some funny stories about sandra, OK?!

jokes.text: Paula to Larry in an aside: Harvey Fierstein's luggage was lost / Larry: 'Do you understand what I'm saying?' / Marylou: 'Yes, they lost his luggage.' / 'Right-o. So you'll be doing Tim Conway's pre-interview on your own. I gotta go find Artie.'
jokes.setup: Paula speaks in a loaded, heavily implied way about Harvey Fierstein's lost luggage as an 'emergency'
jokes.punchline: Marylou takes it completely literally — 'Yes, they lost his luggage' — missing whatever deeper emergency Paula was gesturing at (presumably Fierstein needs specific costuming or items)
jokes.explanation: Marylou's literal-mindedness is a running gag. The luggage situation is clearly a bigger deal than she understands (presumably Fierstein's signature look requires his own clothes), and her cheerful 'Yes, they lost his luggage' captures her cluelessness. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's what my friends used to do, too.

jokes.text: Marylou's calendar mistake: she booked Nicolette Sheridan again tonight because 'It's right there. It's in your handwriting.' / Paula: 'Well, clearly, I wrote it on the wrong day. I didn't know that, so I booked her again.'
jokes.setup: Paula is dealing with multiple show emergencies
jokes.punchline: Marylou has re-booked a guest who was just on the night before — following Paula's own mistaken calendar note — with total confidence
jokes.explanation: Good situational comedy about incompetence compounding on itself — Marylou followed instructions perfectly, but the instructions were wrong. The bureaucratic logic of her defense ('I didn't know that') is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Now my underpants are gonna smell like starbucks.

jokes.text: Marylou to Tim Conway during pre-interview: 'So, OK, you're filming Speed 2.' / Long pause. / 'Anything funny happen between you and Sandra Bullock?'
jokes.setup: Marylou is conducting a professional pre-interview with Tim Conway
jokes.punchline: Her question — implied by the pause and Conway's reaction — is either painfully thin or completely wrong, setting up Conway's escalating frustration
jokes.explanation: Setup moment for Conway's explosion. The implied awkward pause between questions builds dread. Functional but the payoff is elsewhere.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Um, he's fanning my penis right now.

jokes.text: Tim Conway: 'Look, I've done this show a lot. I really have, you know? Quite a few times, so, uh, I don't think there's... it's necessary to go that much in-depth in the pre-interview thing, OK?' / Marylou: 'I know that, but if I just ask—' / Conway: 'Just have Larry ask me about Speed 2, OK?! He'll ask me about Speed 2! I'll fill in! I'll have some funny stories about Sandra, OK?!'
jokes.setup: Marylou is trying to run a proper pre-interview; Conway wants to bypass it
jokes.punchline: Conway's escalating frustration culminating in shouting — 'He'll ask me about Speed 2! I'll fill in!' — a comedy legend reduced to screaming about Sandra Bullock stories
jokes.explanation: A great celebrity-playing-themselves moment — Tim Conway using his real veteran status to dismiss Marylou's pre-interview while also, implicitly, humiliating her. The slow burn to the shout is well-structured cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It's a good thing you don't work at a hardware store, because then it'd be a bad date, as opposed to this where you've dragged me into it.

jokes.text: Marylou to Larry: 'I'm such a big fan of the show. My friends and I used to sit around and get really loaded and watch you all the time.' / Larry: 'That's what my friends used to do, too.'
jokes.setup: Marylou pays a fan compliment to Larry
jokes.punchline: Larry's self-deprecating 'That's what my friends used to do, too' — implying his show requires intoxication to enjoy, or that his friends have abandoned him
jokes.explanation: Excellent Larry line. The ambiguity is the joke — does he mean his friends needed to be drunk to watch, or that his social circle has collapsed? Either reading is dark and funny and very Larry Sanders. Economy is strong. Character-specific: Larry's self-loathing is weaponized.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Conway
dialogue.line: But at this weight horses ask you to get off.

jokes.text: Larry spills his coffee all over himself / Artie: 'That is hot. That is hot. All right. This is good. Now my underpants are gonna smell like Starbucks.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just greeted Nicolette Sheridan and presumably collides with her or has his coffee bumped
jokes.punchline: Larry's resigned 'Now my underpants are gonna smell like Starbucks' — the physical comedy landing in a specific, absurd image
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy is inferred, but the line 'my underpants are gonna smell like Starbucks' is a standout. It's specific (Starbucks, not 'coffee'), self-deprecating (mentioning underpants), and perfectly Larrian in its resigned quality. The specificity elevates this above generic slapstick. Deserves its score.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Conway
dialogue.line: I found that if you rode to the outside fence, then it was much safer, 'cause, you know, sometimes they run into each other on the inside there. It's longer. But it's safer, and I think safety, in this particular instance, is pretty good.

jokes.text: Larry after the coffee spill, seeing Nicolette Sheridan return: 'Nicolette Sheridan's back. Did you see that? You know why? Yes, I think I do know why. I think she likes me.'
jokes.setup: Nicolette Sheridan has returned to the show (because Marylou accidentally re-booked her)
jokes.punchline: Larry's instant romantic interpretation — 'I think she likes me' — oblivious to the actual mundane reason for her return
jokes.explanation: Larry's self-delusion is a signature character trait. His inability to consider any explanation other than romantic interest is funny and consistent. The dramatic irony (we know the real reason) amplifies it.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Conway
dialogue.line: Try not to.

jokes.text: Hank introduces Rayneene on-air: Larry is asked to introduce Hank's date. Hank: 'Um, he's fanning my penis right now. Maybe you better go back to your, uh, seat.'
jokes.setup: Hank has brought a female date to the show as a public image move; Larry is presumably making wind-gesture jokes backstage
jokes.punchline: Hank saying 'he's fanning my penis right now' backstage — the crass aside contrasting with the wholesome image he's trying to project
jokes.explanation: Mildly crude backstage comedy. Hank's crassness in contrast with his performed respectability is functional character comedy. Not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Conway
dialogue.line: I have him in a little tin hut up here in beverly hills, little monkey strapped to his leg and everything, you know, just to kind of keep him active.

jokes.text: Larry on-air about Hank's date: 'It's a good thing you don't work at a hardware store, because then it'd be a bad date, as opposed to this where you've dragged me into it. Honestly, I feel like a third wheel.'
jokes.setup: Larry is being gracious on-air about Hank's request to introduce his date
jokes.punchline: Larry riffs that bringing a date to a TV show is awkward — 'I feel like a third wheel' — with his characteristic mix of wit and self-pity
jokes.explanation: Good Larry on-air riff — warm but edged with genuine irritation. The hardware store non-sequitur is typical Larry Sanders: a joke that starts sharp then trails off slightly. 'I feel like a third wheel' is a reliable laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Cock suck, I don't understand it.

jokes.text: Tim Conway on-air: 'I was gonna be a jockey at one time, when I was younger... You have to weigh about 110 pounds to be a jockey. But at this weight horses ask you to get off.'
jokes.setup: Conway explains he wanted to be a jockey because he was lighter when young
jokes.punchline: 'But at this weight horses ask you to get off' — turning his current weight into a self-deprecating jockey impossibility
jokes.explanation: Solid celebrity-on-talk-show self-deprecating joke. Personalized, economical, clear structure. Conway is a professional comedian and this is his polish showing. The 'horses ask you to get off' image is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, well, it used to be, it's up to 4 bits.

jokes.text: Conway explains his unconventional jockey strategy: 'I found that if you rode to the outside fence, then it was much safer... It's longer.' / Larry (deadpan): 'Oh, jeez.' / Conway: 'But it's safer, and I think safety, in this particular instance, is pretty good.'
jokes.setup: Conway explains that all jockeys crowd the inside fence; he rode the outside
jokes.punchline: The anti-logic of his 'strategy' — go farther to go safer — and his defense 'I think safety, in this particular instance, is pretty good' delivered with total conviction
jokes.explanation: Conway's absurdist horse racing logic is well-constructed — the audience follows the reasoning, sees the flaw, then Conway defends it with 'safety is pretty good.' Larry's deadpan 'Oh, jeez' is the perfect straight-man beat. Conway's persona as a performer who builds elaborate impossible logic is on full display.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Letterman already does that.

jokes.text: Conway on Harvey Korman: 'Do you still see Harvey?' / Conway: 'Try not to.' — then elaborates that he 'got custody' after the show ended and has Harvey in a 'little tin hut... with a little monkey strapped to his leg.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks about Conway's longtime comedy partner Harvey Korman
jokes.punchline: 'Try not to' — then the escalating absurdist description: got custody, tin hut in Beverly Hills, monkey strapped to his leg 'to keep him active'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best celebrity-on-show moments. 'Try not to' as the opener is perfectly deadpan, then Conway escalates to genuinely dark absurdism: 'I got custody of him,' 'little tin hut in Beverly Hills,' 'little monkey strapped to his leg.' The Beverly Hills location makes the tin hut funnier. The monkey detail is absurd enough to be delightful. Conway plays this completely straight, which is his gift. Fully justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Conway
dialogue.line: And I said, 'it's a light bulb, and if you come any closer I'll turn it on.'

jokes.text: Larry pivots: 'So, I understand you've got a nice little part in Speed 2, the movie?' / Conway: 'Excuse me?' / Larry: 'Speed 2? No, uh, not really, no.' / Conway: 'I believe you do have a part in Speed 2.' / Conway: 'I don't think so. I haven't worked in some time. It's pretty much over for me. I mean, it's a wrap.'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to move to a new topic using (again) wrong notes — this time attributing Speed 2 to Tim Conway
jokes.punchline: Conway denies it; Larry insists; Conway escalates to 'I haven't worked in some time. It's pretty much over for me. I mean, it's a wrap.' — an absurdist comic extension that also needles Larry
jokes.explanation: The wrong-notes gag returns with perfect escalation. Conway's 'I don't think so. I haven't worked in some time. It's pretty much over for me.' is brilliant — he commits to the bit completely, using mock despair to embarrass Larry while also being genuinely funny. The escalation from simple denial to existential career crisis is superbly constructed. High rewatch value for anyone who tracked the notes thread.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Conway
dialogue.line: But, guys who had never walked before came running out of that hospital. That's the truth.

jokes.text: Paula backstage, reaction to wrong notes: 'I did! Cock suck, I don't understand it.'
jokes.setup: Larry is looking betrayed at the camera/Artie because the notes are wrong again
jokes.punchline: Paula's explosive backstage profanity — 'Cock suck' — as a reaction to being doubted, unexpected in its vehemence
jokes.explanation: The casual profanity in an HBO show is always a tool, and here it's Paula's character snapping under pressure. The unexpectedness of 'cock suck' as a standalone reaction in backstage chaos is funny. Not refined comedy but it works.

dialogue.speaker: Tim Conway
dialogue.line: I haven't had any sex since the apple dumpling gang, so this is quite a treat.

jokes.text: Larry to Artie: 'What is this, kind of a two-bit show, or something?' / Artie: 'No, well, it used to be, it's up to 4 bits.'
jokes.setup: Conway is grilling Larry on-air about whether the show is properly run
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'No, well, it used to be, it's up to 4 bits' — taking the idiom literally and escalating it arithmetically
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp Artie line. Taking 'two-bit' literally and doubling it to '4 bits' is exactly Artie's comedy register — dry, rapid, self-aware, and with an edge of pride. It's funny because it also contains a real acknowledgment that the show has improved while being completely absurd. Economy is excellent. This is Rip Torn at his best.

dialogue.speaker: Harvey Fierstein
dialogue.line: I know rayneene, well, except when I knew rayneene, she was a man.

jokes.text: Conway's bit reveal on-air: 'Kiddin' ya. Kiddin' ya! Kiddin' ya. I am, I'm in Speed 2.' — then to Larry: 'I was right. I was right.'
jokes.setup: Conway has committed completely to the bit that he has no work and it's all over for him
jokes.punchline: He breaks the bit — 'Kiddin' ya!' — and confirms he IS in Speed 2, which is what Larry said all along
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Conway was pranking Larry — and that Larry was accidentally RIGHT — is a good structural payoff. The 'Kiddin' ya!' repeated three times is Conway's comic rhythm. The role reversal (Larry's wrong notes produced a right answer) is a nice twist.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hank, are you OK?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, no, I'm not. I'm not OK.

jokes.text: Artie backstage to Paula: 'Hey, that would be a good new comedy bit for the show. I'll give Larry the right information, and then the guests will say something different, and then Larry'll act really mad, and then everyone will laugh.' / Paula: 'Letterman already does that.'
jokes.setup: Artie is describing the comedic dynamic they just accidentally created
jokes.punchline: 'Letterman already does that.' — Paula's deadpan dismissal that what Artie is proposing as original is a Letterman staple
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest meta-comedy moments. Artie's proposal is accidentally a real behind-the-scenes insight — this IS a Letterman/talk show comedy device — and Paula's flat 'Letterman already does that' is devastating. It works as a meta-joke about the late-night landscape, a show-business insider joke, and a character joke (Paula as the most practically clear-eyed person in the building). The economy is excellent — four words demolish Artie's idea. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: One of the great moments in television. Talk show, here we come.

jokes.text: Tim Conway on the army: 'I was stationed, uh, in Seattle. I protected Puget Sound for 2 years.' / Larry: 'Congratulations.' / Conway: 'Well, as you know, we were never attacked there.'
jokes.setup: Conway describes his military service
jokes.punchline: 'Well, as you know, we were never attacked there' — taking credit for a non-event with mock pride
jokes.explanation: Conway's logic of 'we were never attacked, and I was there' is perfectly deadpan and the structure (congratulations → 'we were never attacked') is clean. Taking credit for the absence of a catastrophe is a reliable but well-executed comic device. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I don't smell anything, do you?

dialogue.speaker: Nicolette
dialogue.line: Mmm, no. Vanilla latte.

jokes.text: Conway's fluorescent light bulb rifle story: 'I took... one of those long, fluorescent bulbs out of the trash and I pointed that at him. And I said, "Halt. Advance and be recognized." And he did, and he said, "What is that?" And I said, "It's a light bulb, and if you come any closer I'll turn it on."'
jokes.setup: Conway tells a story about losing his rifle while on guard duty and having to improvise
jokes.punchline: 'It's a light bulb, and if you come any closer I'll turn it on' — the absurd non-threat delivered as a serious military warning
jokes.explanation: The episode's funniest stand-up/talk-show-bit moment. Conway's story is brilliantly structured: the setup (lost rifle, lieutenant coming) builds real tension, then the improvisation (fluorescent bulb from trash) is absurd but logical, and the punchline — 'It's a light bulb, and if you come any closer I'll turn it on' — is a masterpiece of absurdist non-threat. The deadpan delivery of an impossibly confident bluff with a light bulb is Conway at his best. Even tagged as standup/celebrity bit, this deserves recognition as exceptional comedy. Fully justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Conway's second court martial story: 'I thought if you put all the coal in, like, at 8:00, you wouldn't have to go around again, you know, later. And, uh, then this hospital went up. But, guys who had never walked before came running out of that hospital. That's the truth.'
jokes.setup: Conway explains he accidentally burned down a hospital by over-stoking the furnace
jokes.punchline: 'But, guys who had never walked before came running out of that hospital. That's the truth.' — finding the silver lining of an arson-adjacent catastrophe
jokes.explanation: Magnificently dark. The logic is absurd (accidentally optimal efficiency in coal-loading leads to hospital fire) but Conway's moral arithmetic — 'but guys who'd never walked before came running out' — is the kind of dark-comic silver lining that makes a room explode. 'That's the truth' as a button, delivered with Conway's innocent authority, is perfect. One of the funniest moments in the episode despite being tagged standup.

jokes.text: Conway: 'Listen, congratulations, I hear you're girlfriend's here tonight.' / Hank says yes. / Conway: 'I haven't had any sex since the Apple Dumpling Gang, so this is quite a treat.'
jokes.setup: Conway transitions to asking Hank about his date in a friendly, warm moment
jokes.punchline: He drops the detail that he hasn't had sex since starring in The Apple Dumpling Gang — a 1975 Disney film — as if this is casually relevant information
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's single best jokes. The comedic payload of 'I haven't had any sex since the Apple Dumpling Gang' is enormous: it uses the real film title (1975 Disney), places his last sexual encounter in the mid-70s, and delivers it with complete casual nonchalance as if reporting a weather condition. The specificity of the Apple Dumpling Gang — a children's movie — makes the sexual context even funnier. This is the kind of joke that gets quoted. Character integration is exceptional (only Tim Conway, playing Tim Conway, could say this). Fully justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Conway on his way out whispers to Larry about Marylou: 'Keep that Marylou away from me.'
jokes.setup: Conway has had to deal with Marylou's incompetent pre-interview
jokes.punchline: His parting shot — whispered, conspiratorial, with the weight of a man who has been through something — perfectly buttons the Marylou thread
jokes.explanation: Good button on the Marylou/Conway thread. The conspiratorial whisper is the right tone — Conway has survived Marylou and wants no more. Economical and character-consistent.

jokes.text: Hank thanks Larry for asking about Rayneene on-air. Larry: 'Should I ask everyone to bring it up?' / Hank: 'Not everyone, but, uh, why, is there a problem?' / Larry: 'It's just that you asked me before the show, and then I did it. And then, you sure that's not enough?' / Hank: 'I mean, that's, uh, enough's enough.'
jokes.setup: Hank is grateful but now worried Larry will over-publicize the beard arrangement
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'enough's enough' — he wanted public attention but now wants to control exactly how much, in classic Hank fashion
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy about Hank's obsessive image management. The exchange reveals Hank's contradictory needs (wants publicity, wants control). Solid but not standout.

jokes.text: Harvey Fierstein enters: 'Larry, Larry, Larry. Last time I said, "Larry, Larry, Larry," it was to Olivier. My life is not going well. How are you?'
jokes.setup: Harvey Fierstein makes his entrance on the show
jokes.punchline: He name-drops Sir Laurence Olivier, then immediately undercuts the grandeur with 'My life is not going well. How are you?' — complete tonal whiplash
jokes.explanation: Harvey Fierstein's entrance is one of the episode's best moments. The Olivier name-drop is simultaneously a legitimate claim (Fierstein is a serious Broadway talent) and absurdly grandiose in this context. Then 'My life is not going well. How are you?' is a perfect non-sequitur pivot that contains both self-deprecation and complete indifference to social pleasantries. Character integration is exceptional — this is only possible with Fierstein playing himself. Fully justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Larry: 'You're frightening at first.' / Fierstein: 'Am I that way to you? Do you see me and go, "oh, my God." You know, "settle down?"' / Larry: 'Well, I'm not used to seeing you with clothes on. I mean my clothes, usually. You know, I watch you at home. I'm laying in bed at night and watching you at home.'
jokes.setup: Larry says Fierstein is 'frightening at first'; Fierstein asks if Larry reacts to him with alarm
jokes.punchline: Larry's recovery — 'I'm not used to seeing you with clothes on. I mean MY clothes' — is an unintentional double entendre that he has to awkwardly walk back
jokes.explanation: Larry's 'I'm not used to seeing you with clothes on' is a classic inadvertent double entendre, especially loaded given the episode's gay-panic subplot. His correction 'I mean MY clothes' then the awkward explanation makes it worse. The cringe is well-earned.

jokes.text: Fierstein: 'I lie in bed and watch the show.' / Larry: 'Now, Harvey... / Fierstein: 'Sometimes the world, it's a small... I know Rayneene. I actually know Rayneene.'
jokes.setup: Fierstein makes small talk; Larry starts to respond; then Fierstein pivots suddenly to reveal he knows Hank's beard date
jokes.punchline: The sudden 'I know Rayneene' after a stumbling sentence fragment is a perfect comic pivot — the half-abandoned 'small world' observation that detonates into something much bigger
jokes.explanation: The structural plant — Larry mid-pivot hearing Rayneene's name from Fierstein — is well-executed. The fragment 'the world, it's a small...' trails off to the reveal, building comedy through truncation. Sets up the episode's biggest bomb.

jokes.text: Fierstein: 'I know Rayneene, well, except when I knew Rayneene, she was a man. But...' / Cut to commercial.
jokes.setup: Fierstein has just said he knows Hank's carefully arranged female date — the one brought specifically to prove Hank is straight
jokes.punchline: '...well, except when I knew Rayneene, she was a man.' — delivered with Fierstein's complete matter-of-fact nonchalance, then immediate cut to commercial
jokes.explanation: The episode's crowning joke and one of the finest comedy moments in the series. Everything pays off simultaneously: Hank's paranoid beard scheme (the Rock Hudson precedent, the Variety column, the gay bars, the denial of visiting Mother Lode) all crashes into the revelation that Rayneene — his chosen proof of heterosexuality — is a trans woman whom Harvey Fierstein knows from her previous life. The punchline is delivered by Harvey Fierstein, the perfect messenger for this content. The cut to commercial immediately after is the final punctuation — the show doesn't milk it, it just drops the bomb and goes to break. Structure is nearly perfect. Character integration is the highest in the episode. Economy: the punchline is twelve words and contains a complete Shakespearean reversal. This is television comedy writing at its best. Fully justified at the top of the scoring range.

jokes.text: Immediate cut to commercial after Fierstein's Rayneene revelation. The cut itself IS the punchline.
jokes.setup: Fierstein has just dropped the bombshell that Rayneene was previously a man
jokes.punchline: Larry's instant 'We'll take a break and come right back' — the fastest commercial cut in talk show history, fleeing the revelation
jokes.explanation: The structural comedy of the instant commercial cut is the episode's defining comedic device used for the second time. Larry's reflexive retreat to the safety of 'we'll take a break' mirrors the Nicolette disaster earlier but with enormously higher stakes. The cut is the joke — what the audience imagines happening in those 90 seconds of commercial is funnier than anything that could be shown. Perfect economy: zero words, maximum impact.

jokes.text: Hank backstage after the Fierstein reveal: 'Oh, no, I'm not. I'm not OK.' / Larry: 'I thought you were, like, doing a bit or something.' / Hank: 'You really didn't know?' / Larry: 'No, I didn't know.'
jokes.setup: The commercial break has ended; Hank is now processing what just happened on live television
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'I thought you were, like, doing a bit or something' — genuinely not knowing — followed by Hank's crushed 'You really didn't know?'
jokes.explanation: The aftermath of the bomb. Larry's 'I thought you were doing a bit' is perfectly calibrated to the show's meta-comedy register — on a talk show, this COULD have been a planned bit. Hank's 'You really didn't know?' contains both the comedy and the tragedy of the episode.

jokes.text: Artie backstage: 'One of the great moments in television. Talk show, here we come.'
jokes.setup: Chaos backstage after the Fierstein revelation
jokes.punchline: Artie's completely calm, professional assessment — 'One of the great moments in television' — as if this catastrophe is merely a career win
jokes.explanation: Artie's eternal producer pragmatism: someone else's disaster is the show's triumph. 'Talk show, here we come' as the button — as if they finally achieved something — is perfect Artie. Character integration is exceptional.

jokes.text: Larry: 'You didn't fire Marylou, did you?' / Artie: 'Want to?'
jokes.setup: In the chaos of the reveal, Larry suddenly worries about Marylou's employment
jokes.punchline: Artie's immediate 'Want to?' — the offer hanging there — is perfect given that Artie has been advocating for her firing the whole episode
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback economy. Artie has been wanting to fire Marylou since minute four; now he offers Larry the option with two words. The contrast between Larry's concern and Artie's eagerness is entirely in character.

jokes.text: Nicolette Sheridan: 'It would've been a pretty tough act to follow.' — about having been bumped by the Fierstein chaos
jokes.setup: Larry apologizes to Nicolette for bumping her segment
jokes.punchline: Nicolette's gracious-but-loaded 'It would've been a pretty tough act to follow' — acknowledging that a transgender revelation live on air is genuinely hard to top
jokes.explanation: An elegant callback button. Nicolette's understatement contains the entire episode in a sentence — yes, that WAS a tough act to follow. Clean, economical, and earns its place as a final grace note.

jokes.text: Larry leans in toward Nicolette: 'I don't smell anything, do you?' / Nicolette: 'Mmm, no. Vanilla latte.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to make a romantic impression on Nicolette Sheridan
jokes.punchline: His anxiety about smelling like coffee (from the earlier spill on his 'underpants') leads to the question; Nicolette confirms 'Vanilla latte' — the coffee spill still very much present
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed callback. Larry's underpants-smell anxiety from joke 41 pays off here: he's trying to impress Nicolette while still smelling like his Starbucks spill. 'Vanilla latte' is the perfect two-word confirmation that absolutely nothing has gone right for Larry in this episode. The episode ends on this note — Larry's romantic aspirations crushed by his own incompetence and coffee. Economy and callback structure are both excellent.

tmdb_overview: Paula's new assistant, Marylou, manages to upset everyone, even the affable Tim Conway, with her ineffective pre-interview techniques and celebrity research. Hank's effort to cheer up a despondent Brian with a night on the town at several gay bars earns him a prominent mention in Army Archerd's column.
